title: Ousted Ukrainian Defense Chief Teams With Palantir CEO on New Venture as Army Secretary Resigns in Pentagon Shakeup
subhead: Mykhailo Fedorov and Alex Karp announced a new defense company, while Army Secretary Dan Driscoll resigned amid friction with Pete Hegseth. Separately, the US cleared an $800M Bell helicopter sale to Iraq and Rheinmetall delivered its first Bradley-replacement prototype.

sections.heading: Fedorov and Palantir's Karp Launch New Defense Venture
sections.body:
Ukraine's ousted defense minister Mykhailo Fedorov is teaming up with Palantir CEO Alex Karp to launch a new defense company focused on technology that will 'ultimately make the world safer,' the pair announced Tuesday, per Defense News. Fedorov left office in July after President Volodymyr Zelenskyy dismissed him, triggering weeks of nationwide protests. Karp, who reached out to Fedorov almost immediately after the dismissal, becomes the venture's first investor.

Karp's backing could mean billions for Ukraine's defense industry. Palantir posted 93% year-over-year revenue growth last quarter, with its valuation above $440 billion — roughly half its revenue from US government contracts. Fedorov built his reputation on Ukraine's Delta battlefield management system, which fuses drone feeds, radar and field data into a real-time command dashboard. Palantir's Maven Smart System, which uses Anthropic's AI model, is the American equivalent. Ukraine's Brave1 Dataroom, a joint defense ministry-Palantir project, already lets Ukrainian firms train AI models on real combat data.
sections.whyItMatters: This formalizes the deep Palantir-Ukraine relationship into a commercial vehicle, giving Fedorov a platform to export Ukraine's wartime drone and AI lessons — and giving Palantir a senior Ukrainian partner with direct access to battlefield-proven technology.

sections.heading: Army Secretary Dan Driscoll Resigns Amid Hegseth Friction
sections.body:
Dan Driscoll, whom President Trump once hailed as 'a disruptor and change agent,' has resigned as secretary of the Army, Defense One reported, citing a source who said Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's purging of generals tied to Driscoll's innovation efforts was a primary cause. The source said Driscoll raised concerns about Army transformation and readiness that Hegseth blocked by firing the responsible generals.

Driscoll's reform agenda, the Army Transformation Initiative launched in May 2025, pushed AI integration into decision-making, pushed purchasing power down the chain of command, and deployed modernized drone formations. Hegseth has already pushed out Army Chief Gen. Randy George, Transformation and Training Command chief Gen. David Hodne, Vice Chief Gen. James Mingus and US Army Europe commander Gen. Christopher Donahue. Sen. Jack Reed said he was 'alarmed' that Driscoll's leadership 'stands in stark contrast to Secretary Hegseth's disastrous tenure.'
sections.whyItMatters: The resignation removes the Army's most visible advocate for Ukraine-style rapid innovation and AI integration, signaling that Hegseth's consolidation of control over the service's transformation agenda is now essentially complete.

sections.heading: US Clears $800M Bell Helicopter Sale to Iraq
sections.body:
The State Department approved a potential $800 million Foreign Military Sale of Bell helicopters, weapons and related equipment to Iraq, Defense News reported. The package covers Bell 412EPX and Bell 407M helicopters (quantities unspecified), GAU-19 three-barrel machine gun launchers, M260 seven-tube launchers for 2.75-inch rockets, L-3 Wescam MX-15HDI electro-optical/infrared sensors and AN/AAR-60 Block 2 missile launch detection systems.

The sale follows a 2026 DoD inspector general report noting Iraq's defense ministry had sought four Bell 412EPXs and 16 Bell 412Ms to replace Russian-made Mi-17 helicopters, plus 15 new Bell 407Ms for the light-attack role. Bell-Textron, based in Fort Worth, Texas, would be the principal contractor. The notification is approval of a possible sale, not a completed contract — final quantity and cost could change.
sections.whyItMatters: The deal continues Iraq's shift away from Russian rotary-wing platforms toward US systems, a quiet but steady erosion of Moscow's remaining arms foothold in the Middle East.

sections.heading: Rheinmetall Delivers First Bradley-Replacement Prototype
sections.body:
American Rheinmetall delivered the first Lynx XM30 prototype to the Army this week, Defense News reported, the latest step in the service's effort to replace the M2 Bradley Fighting Vehicle. The vehicle is slated to start testing, with seven additional prototypes due later this year under a roughly $764 million Engineering and Manufacturing Development contract.

The XM30, built on Rheinmetall's Lynx KF41, was designed for a battlefield shaped by drones and electronic warfare, with modular open architecture for quick technology integration and a first-of-its-kind hybrid-electric powertrain. The Army plans a 'parallel evaluation timeline' — technical testing while soldiers train with additional prototypes. In 2023, the Army selected American Rheinmetall and General Dynamics Land Systems for the XM30 design phase.
sections.whyItMatters: The prototype delivery moves the Army's flagship ground-vehicle modernization from design to hardware, with the hybrid-electric powertrain and open architecture signaling how the service expects future armored vehicles to counter drone and EW threats.

sections.heading: GAO: Navy Subs Idle for Years as Shipyards Overload
sections.body:
Maintenance delays have cost the Navy's attack submarine fleet more than 41 ship-years of operation, and boats waiting to be decommissioned could cost over $3 billion in the next five years, according to a Government Accountability Office report released Aug. 27 and covered by Defense One. The core problem: shipyards are overloaded with work.

The USS Pasadena entered inactive idle status on Jan. 1, 2025 and is not expected to be inducted into Norfolk Naval Shipyard for decommissioning until Nov. 15, 2028 — 1,414 days — costing about $300 million in operating and support costs. Without mitigation, 15 attack submarines will enter inactive idle time from FY2026 through FY2030, incurring more than 14,000 idle days and $3.1 billion. Over the past decade the Navy spent about $3.3 billion on idle Los Angeles-class boats and $835 million on idle Virginia-class boats — roughly $230,000 for every day a sub sits pierside. The GAO recommended alternative decommissioning options, including defueling outside drydocks and reducing crewing.
sections.whyItMatters: The report quantifies a structural bottleneck in the US submarine industrial base: the Navy is paying billions to keep boats idle it cannot get into shipyards, even as it races to expand the fleet against China's naval buildup.

sections.heading: US Components Still Flowing Into Russian Ballistic Missiles
sections.body:
Dozens of American- and European-made components are still being used to build Russia's ballistic missiles despite nearly 24,000 sanctions imposed since 2022, Ukraine's presidential commissioner for sanctions policy said, per Defense News. Vladyslav Vlasiuk displayed parts recovered from Iskander missiles and 48N6-family rounds fired from S-400 launchers, with guidance and navigation components traced to the US, Japan, Germany, Taiwan, France, Britain and Switzerland.

'The United States is the leader,' Vlasiuk said, noting ballistic missiles are especially demanding on component quality. A 2024 investigation found roughly 70% of foreign components in Russian missiles came from US companies. Russian makers source sensitive electronics through third-country intermediaries that can be replaced almost as quickly as they are sanctioned, including components from Nvidia, Texas Instruments, Analog Devices and Microchip Technology. Kyiv wants partners to synchronize designations on Russian ballistic manufacturers, impose sectoral restrictions on roughly 110 missile-production materials, and tighten export licensing.
sections.whyItMatters: The disclosure underscores the limits of sanctions enforcement on Russia's missile supply chain — and comes as Russia ramps ballistic and high-speed missile production to more than 100 a month while allies face a 'dire' interceptor shortage.

sections.heading: US Resumes Strikes on Iran Around Strait of Hormuz
sections.body:
The US launched new air strikes on Iranian targets Tuesday, quashing hopes that a weekend exchange might not lead to a wider renewal of hostilities, Reuters reported. US Central Command said forces began striking IRGC targets after attempted attacks against commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and American service members. Iran's state media reported explosions on Qeshm Island and in Bandar Abbas, Chabahar, Jask and Sirik.

Brent crude futures, already up 2% on the day, jumped almost 2% more on reports of two tankers being hit leaving the strait. Tehran warned it would prevent oil exports from the Gulf, while President Trump threatened to hit Iran 'hard' in response to renewed strikes and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Washington was about to impose new sanctions. The six-month-old conflict had shifted in recent weeks, with the US and Iran pausing mutual strikes in late July before this week's resumption.
sections.whyItMatters: The resumption of direct US-Iran strikes reopens the risk to Gulf oil flows and global interceptor stocks, compounding the munitions-drain and supply-chain pressures already straining Western defense production.

bottomLine: Today's defense news was dominated by personnel and industry moves rather than a single procurement headline: Ukraine's ousted defense chief formalized a commercial partnership with Palantir's Alex Karp, Army Secretary Dan Driscoll resigned amid Hegseth's purge of transformation-focused generals, the US cleared an $800M Bell helicopter sale to Iraq, and Rheinmetall delivered its first Bradley-replacement prototype. Underneath, the GAO's submarine-idle report and the disclosure of US components in Russian missiles both point to the same theme — capacity and supply-chain constraints are the binding constraint on Western defense, even as the US-Iran conflict around Hormuz resumes and tightens the pressure on munitions and interceptor stocks.
sources: Defense News, Defense One, Reuters, GAO, State Department
